summary: An animal is mu'ad to break things with its feet as it walks, so the owner pays in full. If it kicks or sends pebbles flying, he pays half. Chickens have the same rules.
stIntro: The mishna in the previous chapter (15b) teaches that the owner of an animal is always forewarned with regard to the category of Trampling.

chunks.en: How is the foot mu'ad?
chunks.st: The mishna elaborates: For what damage caused with the hoof is the animal deemed forewarned?

chunks.en: To break things as it walks.
chunks.st: It is deemed forewarned with regard to trampling objects and breaking them in the course of its walking.

chunks.en: An animal is mu'ad to walk the usual way and break things.
chunks.st: An animal is deemed forewarned with regard to walking in its typical manner and, by doing so, breaking objects as it proceeds.

chunks.en: If it was kicking,
chunks.st: By contrast, if the animal was kicking while it was walking,

chunks.en: or pebbles were flying out from under
chunks.st: or it transpired that pebbles were inadvertently propelled from under its

chunks.en: its feet and broke the dishes,
chunks.st: feet and those pebbles broke vessels,
chunks.stMore: cases of that kind do not fit precisely into the primary category of Trampling.

chunks.en: the owner pays half the damage.
chunks.st: In both of these cases the owner of the animal pays half the cost of the damage.

chunks.en: If it stepped on a dish and broke it,
chunks.st: If an animal trod upon a vessel and broke it and then a shard of that vessel

chunks.en: and a piece fell on another dish and broke it,
chunks.st: fell upon a second vessel and broke it,

chunks.en: for the first dish he pays the full damage,
chunks.st: the owner pays the full cost of the damage for the first vessel,
chunks.stMore: as its action is classified under the primary category of Trampling,

chunks.en: and for the last one he pays half the damage.
chunks.st: and he pays half the cost of the damage for the latter vessel,
chunks.stMore: as the damage caused by the shard is tantamount to damage caused by pebbles inadvertently propelled by the foot of an animal.

chunks.en: Chickens are mu'ad to walk the usual way and break things.
chunks.st: Chickens are deemed forewarned with regard to walking in their typical manner and breaking objects,
chunks.stMore: and therefore, the owner of a chicken pays the full restitution for the damage done to any objects broken by his chicken.

chunks.en: If a string was tied to its leg,
chunks.st: If there was a string [delil] tied to a chicken’s leg
chunks.stMore: as an indication of ownership and it wrapped around a vessel and broke it,

chunks.he: אוֹ שֶׁהָיָה מְהַדֵּס וּמְשַׁבֵּר אֶת הַכֵּלִים,
chunks.en: or it was hopping and breaking the dishes,
chunks.st: or if the chicken was hopping in an atypical manner and breaking vessels,

chunks.en: the owner pays half the damage.
chunks.st: its owner pays half the cost of the damage.

summary: An animal is mu'ad to eat fruits and vegetables, so if it eats them on someone else's land the owner pays in full. In the street he does not pay, except for the benefit the animal got from eating.

chunks.en: How is the tooth mu'ad?
chunks.st: Within the context of the primary category of Eating, for what damage caused with the tooth is an animal deemed forewarned?

chunks.en: To eat what is fit for it.
chunks.st: It is deemed forewarned with regard to eating food items fit for its consumption.

chunks.en: An animal is mu'ad to eat fruits and vegetables.
chunks.st: The domesticated animal is deemed forewarned with regard to eating fruits and vegetables.

chunks.en: If it ate clothing or dishes,
chunks.st: If the animal ate garments or vessels,

chunks.en: the owner pays half the damage.
chunks.st: the owner pays half the cost of the damage.
chunks.stMore: As these are not items fit for its consumption, the animal is not deemed forewarned in this case.

chunks.en: When is this said?
chunks.explain: When does the owner pay in full for food it ate?
chunks.st: In what case is this statement applied, that one pays the full value of the food eaten by the animal?

chunks.en: On the land of the one who was hurt.
chunks.st: It is a case where the animal ate the food on the property of the injured party;

chunks.en: But in the street, where everyone walks,
chunks.st: but if the animal ate food in the public domain,

words.note: The public: streets and places everyone uses.

chunks.en: he does not pay. But if the animal got some benefit,
chunks.st: the owner of the animal is exempt from liability. And even if the animal ate food in the public domain, if the animal derives benefit from eating another’s produce in the public domain,

words.note: He does not have to pay.

chunks.en: he pays for the benefit it got.
chunks.st: the owner pays for the benefit that it derives, just not for the full cost of the food.

chunks.en: How does he pay for the benefit it got?
chunks.st: Under what circumstances does the owner of the animal pay for the benefit that it derives?

chunks.en: If it ate from the middle of the square,
chunks.st: If the animal ate produce in the public square in the area before the storefronts,

words.note: The open area in front of the stores.

chunks.en: he pays for the benefit it got.
chunks.st: the owner of the animal pays for the benefit that it derives.

chunks.en: From the sides of the square,
chunks.st: If the animal ate from food placed at the side of the public square,
chunks.stMore: which is not a public thoroughfare,

chunks.en: he pays for what it damaged.
chunks.st: the owner of the animal pays for what it damaged,
chunks.stMore: as the legal status of that area is like that of the property of the injured party.

chunks.en: From the doorway of the store,
chunks.st: If the animal ate produce from the entrance of the store,

chunks.en: he pays for the benefit it got.
chunks.st: its owner pays for the benefit that it derives,
chunks.stMore: as the status of a store entrance is like that of the public domain.

chunks.en: From inside the store,
chunks.st: If the animal ate produce from inside the store,

chunks.en: he pays for what it damaged.
chunks.st: its owner pays for what it damaged.

summary: A dog or goat that jumps off a roof and breaks things: the owner pays in full. A dog that carries a burning cake to a pile of grain and sets it on fire: he pays in full for the cake and half for the grain.

chunks.en: A dog or a goat that jumped from the top of
chunks.st: With regard to a dog or a goat that jumped from

chunks.en: the roof and broke the dishes,
chunks.st: a rooftop and broke vessels while doing so,

chunks.en: the owner pays the full damage,
chunks.st: their owners must pay the full cost of the damage to the vessels

chunks.en: because they are mu'ad.
chunks.st: because these animals are deemed forewarned concerning to jumping.

chunks.en: A dog that took a hot cake and went to a pile of grain,
chunks.explain: The cake was baked on hot coals.
chunks.st: With regard to a dog that took a cake that had been baked directly on hot coals, and went to a stack of grain to eat it,

words.note: A cake baked right on hot coals.

chunks.en: ate the cake, and set the pile on fire.
chunks.explain: A hot coal came along with the cake.
chunks.st: and it ate the cake and at the same time ignited the stack of grain with a coal that it had taken along with the cake,

chunks.en: For the cake he pays the full damage,
chunks.st: the owner of the dog must pay the full cost of the damage for the cake,

chunks.en: and for the pile he pays half the damage.
chunks.st: and he must pay for half the cost of the damage to the stack of grain.

summary: When does an ox become mu'ad, and when does it go back to being tam? Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir disagree.

chunks.en: Which ox is tam,
chunks.st: Which type of ox is deemed innocuous

chunks.en: and which is mu'ad?
chunks.st: and which is deemed forewarned?

chunks.he: מוּעָד, כֹּל שֶׁהֵעִידוּ בוֹ שְׁלשָׁה יָמִים.
chunks.en: Mu'ad: any ox that witnesses said gored on three days.
chunks.st: An ox is deemed forewarned in any case where witnesses testified about it that it gored on three different days.

chunks.en: And it is tam again once it stops goring for three days.
chunks.st: And it reverts back to its previous innocuous status from when it reverses its behavior and refrains from goring for three consecutive days;

chunks.en: These are the words of Rabbi Yehuda.
chunks.st: this is the statement of Rabbi Yehuda.

chunks.en: Rabbi Meir says,
chunks.st: Rabbi Meir says:

chunks.en: Mu'ad: one that witnesses said gored three times.
chunks.st: It is deemed forewarned in any case where witnesses testified that it gored three times,
chunks.stMore: regardless of the number of days on which this behavior occurred.

chunks.en: And tam: when children pet it
chunks.st: And it reverts back to its previous innocuous status in any case where children pet it

chunks.en: and it does not gore.
chunks.st: and play with it and it does not gore them.

summary: If an ox gores on someone else's land, Rabbi Tarfon says the owner pays in full, and the Sages say half. Rabbi Tarfon tries to prove it from the rules of tooth and foot, and the Sages answer with the rule of "dayo".

chunks.en: What is an ox that damages on the land of the one it hurt?
chunks.st: And what is the case of the ox that causes damage while on the property of the injured party,
chunks.stMore: mentioned in an earlier mishna (15b) that listed animals that are forewarned?

chunks.en: If it gored, pushed,
chunks.st: If the animal gored, pushed,

chunks.en: bit, lay down on things,
chunks.st: bit, squatted upon, or

chunks.en: or kicked, in the street,
chunks.st: kicked another animal in the public domain,

chunks.en: the owner pays half the damage.
chunks.st: the owner is liable to pay half the cost of the damage if the ox was innocuous,

chunks.en: On the land of the one who was hurt,
chunks.st: but if it acted while on the property of the injured party,

chunks.en: Rabbi Tarfon says: full damage.
chunks.st: Rabbi Tarfon says: He must pay the full cost of the damage,

chunks.en: And the Sages say: half damage.
chunks.st: and the Rabbis say: He must pay half the cost of the damage,
chunks.stMore: as in any other case classified as Goring.

chunks.en: Rabbi Tarfon said to them:
chunks.st: Rabbi Tarfon said to the Rabbis:

chunks.en: Where the Torah was easy on the tooth
chunks.st: If in a place where the Torah was lenient with regard to damage classified as Eating

chunks.en: and the foot, in the street,
chunks.st: and with regard to Trampling, specifically in the public domain,

chunks.en: that the owner does not pay,
chunks.st: as the owner is exempt from liability,

chunks.en: it was strict with them on the land of the one who was hurt,
chunks.st: nevertheless the Torah was strict with regard to these forms of damage if they occurred on the property of the injured party,

chunks.en: to pay full damage.
chunks.st: requiring him to pay the full cost of the damage,

chunks.he: מְקוֹם שֶׁהֶחְמִיר עַל הַקֶּרֶן בִּרְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים,
chunks.en: So where it was strict about the horn in the street,
chunks.st: then in a place where the Torah was strict with regard to cases of damage classified as Goring, specifically in the public domain,

chunks.en: to pay half damage,
chunks.st: requiring the owner liable to pay for half the cost of the damage,

chunks.en: isn't it right that we be strict with it on the land
chunks.st: is it not right that we should be strict with regard to this form of damage if it occurs

chunks.en: of the one who was hurt, to pay full damage?
chunks.st: on the property of the injured party to likewise require the owner of the animal to pay the full cost of the damage?

chunks.en: They said to him:
chunks.st: The Rabbis said to him:

chunks.he: דַּיּוֹ לַבָּא מִן הַדִּין לִהְיוֹת כַּנִּדּוֹן,
chunks.en: It is enough for what we learn to be like what we learn it from.
chunks.explain: This rule is called "dayo": it is enough.
chunks.st: Although there is an a fortiori inference being applied here, still it is sufficient for the conclusion that emerges from an a fortiori inference to be like its source,
chunks.stMore: meaning that the halakha cannot be stricter with the inference than it is with the case that serves as the source of the inference.

chunks.en: Just as in the street it is half damage,
chunks.st: Therefore, just as one is liable to pay half the cost of the damage classified as Goring in the public domain,

chunks.en: so too on the land of the one who was hurt, half damage.
chunks.st: so too, for damage classified as Goring on the property of the injured party he is liable to pay only half the cost of the damage.

chunks.en: He said to them:
chunks.st: Rabbi Tarfon said to them:

chunks.en: I will not learn horn from horn;
chunks.st: If that is your opinion, then I as well will not derive an inference with regard to Goring from a different case of Goring.

chunks.en: I will learn horn from foot.
chunks.st: I will instead derive an inference with regard to Goring from Trampling:

chunks.en: Where the Torah was easy on
chunks.st: And if in a place where the Torah was lenient with regard to damage classified as

chunks.en: the tooth and the foot
chunks.st: Eating and Trampling,

chunks.en: in the street,
chunks.st: specifically in the public domain, as the owner is exempt from liability,

chunks.en: it was strict with the horn,
chunks.st: nevertheless the Torah was strict with regard to damage classified as Goring, requiring him to pay half the cost of the damage,

chunks.he: מְקוֹם שֶׁהֶחְמִיר עַל הַשֵּׁן וְעַל הָרֶגֶל,
chunks.en: so where it was strict with the tooth and the foot
chunks.st: then in a place where the Torah was strict with regard to damage classified as Eating and Trampling,

chunks.en: on the land of the one who was hurt,
chunks.st: specifically on the property of the injured party as the animal’s owner is obligated to pay the full cost of the damage,

chunks.en: isn't it right that we be strict with the horn?
chunks.st: is it not right that we should be equally strict with regard to damage classified as Goring and require payment of the full cost of the damage in this case as well?

chunks.en: They said to him:
chunks.st: The Rabbis said to him: Here as well,

chunks.he: דַּיּוֹ לַבָּא מִן הַדִּין לִהְיוֹת כַּנִּדּוֹן,
chunks.en: It is enough for what we learn to be like what we learn it from.
chunks.st: it is sufficient for the conclusion that emerges from an a fortiori inference to be like its source,

chunks.en: Just as in the street it is half damage,
chunks.st: and therefore, just as one is liable to pay half the cost of the damage classified as Goring in the public domain,

chunks.en: so too on the land of the one who was hurt, half damage.
chunks.st: so too, for damage classified as Goring on the property of the injured party he will be liable to pay only half the cost of the damage,
chunks.stMore: as ultimately your inference still depends on the fact that for Goring in the public domain one pays half the cost of the damage.

summary: A person is always mu'ad. Whatever damage he does, by accident or on purpose, awake or asleep, he pays in full.

chunks.en: A person is always mu'ad,
chunks.st: The legal status of a person is always that of one forewarned.

chunks.en: whether by accident,
chunks.st: Therefore, whether the damage was unintentional

chunks.en: or on purpose,
chunks.st: or intentional,

chunks.en: whether awake,
chunks.st: whether he was awake while he caused the damage

chunks.en: or asleep.
chunks.st: or asleep, whether

chunks.en: If he blinded his friend's eye
chunks.st: he blinded another’s eye

chunks.en: or broke the dishes,
chunks.st: or broke vessels,

chunks.en: he pays the full damage.
chunks.st: he must pay the full cost of the damage.
